The eve of the wedding

Friday, 30 April 2037, evening, on the veranda of Grandma’s country house near Iași. The house has been renovated by the Bucharest office of Fabre & Popescu. Tomorrow Sorina and Andrei are getting married here, under the lime tree. Viorica has come from Bucharest.
Everything must be ready before the guests arrive. The chairs, the flowers, the lanterns in the lime tree…
Calm down. Once we’ve set out the chairs, there’ll only be the lanterns left.
If someone had told me in 1950 that one day I’d come to a wedding in Moldavia at ninety-six, I wouldn’t have believed it.
The doctor had said you wouldn’t be able to make the journey.
Doctors say a lot of things. I wanted my grandson to get married in front of me. And I wanted to meet this grandmother who whistles so loudly.
She said she’d come tomorrow morning, as soon as her son-in-law had fixed the car.
Let’s hope he’s a good mechanic. At our age, we no longer have time to wait.
I’m sorry not all my colleagues from Lyon came. They would have loved this house.
Ioana is here, Julien too, and the whole family. Nobody important is missing.
Yes, someone is. My father would have wanted to play for you. He would have chosen a Chopin waltz.
Then tomorrow, before we say yes, I’ll play Henri’s waltz. And you’ll play three notes.
With one finger. And the grandmother from Iași will play three more, with two fingers. I promised to teach her.
(he laughs) Once you’ve both finished, all we’ll have left to do is dance.

1. Indicative or subjunctive?
A review of the basic rules from B1–B2:
il faut que, je veux que, je souhaite que
je sais que, je suis sûr que, il est évident que
je regrette que, je suis content que, j’ai peur que
j’espère que, je pense que (affirmative)
je ne pense pas que, je doute que
je crois que, il me semble que
bien que, pour que, avant que, pourvu que, à condition que
parce que, pendant que, après que, alors que, depuis que
Classic traps: “j’espère que” + INDICATIVE (“j’espère qu’il viendra”), but “je souhaite que” + SUBJUNCTIVE. “Après que” + INDICATIVE, but “avant que” + SUBJUNCTIVE.
2. Sequence of tenses
When the main verb is in the past, the tenses in reported speech “move one step back”:
Reported speech (after “il a dit que”)
« Je viens. » (present)
qu’il venait (imperfect)
« Je suis venu. » (passé composé)
qu’il était venu (pluperfect)
« Je viendrai. » (future)
qu’il viendrait (present conditional)
« J’aurai fini. » (future perfect)
qu’il aurait fini (past conditional)
Elle a dit qu’elle viendrait demain matin, dès que son gendre aurait réparé la voiture. = She said: “I’ll come tomorrow morning, as soon as my son-in-law has fixed the car.”
3. The future perfect

The future perfect (auxiliary in the future + participle) expresses an action that will be COMPLETED before another one in the future. After “quand, dès que, lorsque, une fois que” French uses the future, not the present as English does:
Once we’ve set out the chairs, the lanterns will be left.
As soon as he’s fixed the car, she’ll come.
At midnight they will have been married for six hours.
Typical mistake: “Quand je finis, je t’appelle” for the future ✗ → “Quand j’aurai fini, je t’appellerai” ✓.
4. The past conditional
The past conditional (auxiliary in the conditional + participle) expresses a regret, a reproach or an unreal hypothesis in the past. In the “si” clause you use the PLUPERFECT:
If someone had told me that in 1950, I wouldn’t have believed it.
They would have loved this house. (regret)
You should have warned me! (reproach)
According to the press, the minister has reportedly resigned. (unconfirmed information)
Never the conditional after hypothetical “si”: “Si j’aurais su” ✗ → “Si j’avais su” ✓.
5. Passé simple: recognition only
In literature and historical texts you will meet the passé simple. You don’t need to use it, but you must recognise it:

Le tilleul de 1946

Sorina and Andrei had got engaged in front of the Maison Stan piano in May 2035. It took them two years to choose where to marry. Andrei wanted Bucharest, because of his great-grandfather. Sorina wanted Cluj, because of her mother. Doina wanted Cotroceni, because of her kitchen. And Grandma, from Iași, kept telling anyone who would listen on the phone that she was the oldest and no longer travelled, and that consequently the wedding would take place in Moldavia.

Grandma had waged a real campaign. She called Sorina every Sunday to remind her of her age. She called Andrei every Wednesday to remind him she would never take the train again. She had even called Doina, whom she had never met, to explain that Moldavian sarmale were better than Bucharest ones. Doina hung up. Then she called back to defend her recipe for an hour. The two women now argued on the phone every week. Sorina said they had become friends without noticing.

It was Ioana who found the solution. One autumn evening in 2036 she called Sorina and told her about the village house near Iași, the one whose red-ribboned key Grandma had given her for her ninetieth birthday. The house had been empty for years. The roof leaked. The windows no longer shut. But in front of the door stood a ninety-year-old lime tree, planted the day Grandma was born. Ioana said: “What if we repaired it?”

Sorina had first gone to see the house in November with Ioana, in cold rain. She opened the door with the red-ribboned key. Inside, everything was damp and dark. The cat Henri-Ion had found the year before still lived under the veranda. It watched them come in with the air of an offended owner. Sorina went round the rooms taking notes. At the end she said it was the most beautiful house she had ever seen, and the most damaged.

Sorina had been running the Bucharest office of Fabre & Popescu for a year. She had a team of six architects and craftsmen, all Romanian, who restored old houses all over the country. She said yes at once. It would be Ioana’s wedding present: Grandma’s house, renovated, so that the wedding could take place under the lime tree. And afterwards the house would stay in the family, for summers, as Grandma had wished. When Grandma was told about the project, she cried on the phone for five minutes.

Sorina’s team included an old carpenter from the neighbouring village, Ion, seventy-four, who had known Grandma as a child. They went to the same school, three kilometres away, on foot, in the snow. Ion rebuilt the veranda piece by piece with tools inherited from his grandfather. He said he was rebuilding it exactly as it had been in 1952, when Grandma was six and stole an apple from him in this garden. He had never forgiven her. He laughed as he told the story.

The work had begun in March 2037, as soon as the snow melted. Sorina’s team redid the roof, in tiles this time, instead of the old rusty tin. They replaced the windows but kept the old wooden shutters, which Sorina had repainted blue, the same blue as the veranda. Inside they restored the tiled stove, cleaned the parquet and whitewashed the walls. And on the main wall, in pride of place, they hung the old photo of Grandma’s parents on their wedding day in 1938.

Clearing out the attic, the workers found a small wooden box hidden under a beam. Inside was a schoolgirl’s exercise book from 1953, covered in clumsy drawings and Romanian sentences written with great care. On the first page were a name and an age: Grandma’s, seven years old. Sorina didn’t open it any further. She put it back in the box. She decided to give it to Grandma on the wedding day, under the lime tree.

There was still the problem of the piano. Sorina wanted to play the waltz on the wedding day, but there was obviously no piano in a Moldavian village at the end of a dirt track. Mr Petrescu solved the problem. He knew the director of the Iași music school, who had an old upright piano nobody used any more. Mr Petrescu restored it in three weeks. Then he had it taken to the village in a van, holding it himself the whole way, sitting in the back, like a sick child.

The dirt track was so bad that the van got stuck in the mud five hundred metres from the house. It took six village men, two horses and a tractor to pull it out. Mr Petrescu didn’t let go of the piano for a second. When they finally reached the house, he opened the lid, played a chord, and declared very seriously that the piano hadn’t moved by a semitone. The villagers looked at him the way you look at a magician.

Meanwhile Andrei had left London for good. He now worked as an engineer in Bucharest for a company that built schools. He spent his weekends at the Maison Stan with his grandmother and drove out to the village every fortnight to help Sorina on site. He had learnt to lay tiles with Ion the carpenter. Ion said he was the worst roofer in Moldavia but the most enthusiastic. Andrei took it as a compliment.

The hardest part, though, had been Viorica. She was ninety-six. She hardly ever left the Maison Stan, where she spent her days in her armchair by her father’s piano, listening to the music school pupils. Her doctor had said that a seven-hour train journey to Iași, followed by an hour by car on a dirt track, was simply impossible. Viorica listened to the doctor politely. Then she asked him whether he had grandchildren. He said yes. She said: “Then you understand.”

Viorica hadn’t left Bucharest for more than thirty years. On the train she looked out of the window for hours without speaking: the plains, the villages, the wooden churches, the horse-drawn carts still seen on the small roads. She told Ilinca she had never seen Moldavia. That she had spent her whole life in one city, almost in one house. That it had taken her ninety-six years to make this journey. She said it was never too late to see a new country, even when it was your own.

She made the journey on Thursday 29 April, in a first-class compartment the music school pupils had decorated with paper flowers. Ilinca had come from Madrid to accompany her. So had Mr Petrescu, who had brought a flask of coffee and an accordion to pass the time. They played the waltz three times during the journey, to the great surprise of the other passengers. The third time, a ticket inspector whistled the three notes before asking for their tickets.

At Iași station, Elena was waiting on the platform with a bunch of lilac and a car lent by a neighbour. Grandma hadn’t come. She had sent word that she preferred to meet Viorica under the lime tree, not on a station platform, because it was more dignified for two ladies of their age. Viorica laughed. She said she understood perfectly and would have done exactly the same. She added that she was already beginning to love this woman.

The Lyon group had arrived the same day, by plane to Iași. There were many of them. Julien and Ioana, who would be the wedding godparents. Rose-Hélène, who had turned nine in March and would be bridesmaid. Henri-Ion, six, in charge of the rings, which worried Ioana greatly. Isabelle. Haruka, with her violin. Amina, Bertrand and Awa, who was nearly one and walking everywhere now, often falling over. And Farid, whom Sorina had invited on hearing his story, and who had never been to a wedding in his life.

For Farid, this was his first plane journey since arriving in France. He had hesitated a long time before accepting. He was afraid of airports, of checks, of papers looked at for too long. Ioana went with him everywhere: the desk, security, boarding. When the plane took off, Farid closed his eyes and clutched his little stone. Rose-Hélène, sitting next to him, played him the three notes on the harmonica, very softly. He opened his eyes again.

Haruka had spent the whole of April learning Romanian tunes with Ilinca by video, between classes at the conservatoire. Ilinca sent her recordings of old Moldavian songs, and Haruka learnt them by ear in the evenings, in Odile’s room. Mr Delattre, her teacher, heard her one day in the corridor. He asked her what it was. She explained. He said it was the best way to learn music: like a language, by listening to those who have always spoken it.

Ioana had explained to the Lyon group the Romanian tradition of the godparents, the “nași”. They weren’t mere witnesses. They were guides, protectors, almost second parents for the couple. They paid part of the wedding, held the candles during the religious ceremony, and had to watch over the couple all their lives. Later they would also be the children’s godparents. Julien asked whether it was a big responsibility. Ioana said it was the biggest of all, after being a parent.

When they arrived at the village house on Thursday evening, Elena was waiting at the door with a big round loaf and a little dish of salt on an embroidered cloth. Ioana explained it was the Romanian tradition for welcoming guests: bread and salt. Each person had to break off a piece of bread, dip it in the salt and eat it. Farid was the last. He said that in Afghanistan too, sharing bread and salt meant you would never be strangers again. Elena kissed him on both cheeks.

On Friday everyone worked at the village house. The village women had come to help, as tradition required, with baskets, pots and embroidered tablecloths. Elena ran the kitchen. Doina, who had arrived from Cotroceni with forty kilos of cabbage, made sarmale by the hundred. Haruka and Rose-Hélène hung paper lanterns in the branches of the lime tree. Farid, who didn’t know what to do, ended up carrying tables with the village men. He didn’t speak Romanian. He said he didn’t need to in order to carry tables.

The village children were fascinated by Haruka and Farid. They had never seen a Japanese woman or an Afghan man. They followed them everywhere, whispering. Haruka eventually took her violin out in the courtyard and played them the three notes of the waltz. Then she taught them to whistle them. After an hour, twenty children were whistling off-key round the lime tree, watched fondly by their mothers. Farid taught them a game from his childhood, with little pebbles. The children learnt it in ten minutes. They beat him hollow.

On Friday evening on the veranda, Viorica sat for a long time in an armchair, wrapped in her violet shawl, looking at the lime tree. She talked with Sorina and Andrei about her father, the piano, and the Chopin waltz he would have wanted to play. She said that if someone had told her in 1950 that one day she would come to a wedding in Moldavia at ninety-six, she wouldn’t have believed it. Then she asked what time the grandmother who whistled so loudly would arrive. Andrei said she would come the next morning, as soon as Dan had fixed the car.

On Friday evening the village men roasted two lambs on a spit at the bottom of the garden, over a wood fire. They turned them all night, taking turns, drinking țuică and singing old songs. Julien and Bertrand wanted to join in. They were given the spit for an hour, around two in the morning. They talked about music, their fathers, their daughters. Bertrand said he had never spent a night like it in his life. Julien said neither had he. The lambs were perfect.

On Saturday 1 May the weather was glorious. The sky was a perfect blue, without a cloud, and the lime tree, which had started to flower the week before, scented the whole courtyard. At nine o’clock an old red car came jolting up the dirt track, belching black smoke. It stopped in front of the house. Dan got out of the driver’s side, covered in grease up to his elbows. Then the back door opened. And Grandma got out, in her blue dress, leaning on her cane, with a broad smile.

Meanwhile, in the house, the bride was being dressed. It was a tradition, Ioana explained: the women of the family gathered round the bride and sang old songs while her hair was done and her veil put on. Doina cried as she sang. Elena sang off-key. Rose-Hélène held the pins. And when Doina placed the veil on her daughter’s head, all the women fell silent at once, without being asked. Eight seconds. Then Doina said: “There. You’re ready.”

She was ninety-one. She hadn’t seen her childhood home since the year before, when it was still a ruin. She stopped in the middle of the courtyard. She looked at the new roof, the blue shutters, the veranda, the lanterns in the lime tree. She said nothing for a long time. Then she said, in Romanian, a sentence Ioana translated for the Lyon group: “It’s exactly as it was when I was six. Only better.” She turned to Sorina, kissed her and told her she was the best architect in Romania.

On the other side of the door, another tradition awaited Andrei. The village children were blocking his way, holding hands. To go in and fetch the bride, he had to “buy her back” by paying the children in coins and sweets. Henri-Ion had joined the village children without anyone asking him. He demanded chocolate, in French, very firmly. Andrei had to negotiate for ten minutes. He ended up handing over everything in his pockets, including his car keys, which Ioana discreetly retrieved.

Then she saw Viorica on the veranda, in her armchair. The two old ladies looked at each other. They had never met. They had only seen each other on screens, in videos, for two years. Grandma crossed the courtyard slowly with her cane. Viorica tried to stand. Ilinca helped her. They found themselves face to face at the foot of the veranda steps. And Grandma, instead of saying hello, whistled three notes. Very loudly. Very off-key. Viorica burst out laughing. Then she answered, whistling too, even more off-key.

They hugged for a long time in the middle of the courtyard, watched by everyone. Then they sat side by side on the veranda, in two armchairs Dan had brought, and began talking in Romanian, very fast, both at once, like two old friends reunited after years. They talked about their husbands, their fathers, 1950, communism, queues, their grandchildren. Ioana said she had never seen her grandmother talk so fast. Julien said he had never seen Viorica laugh so much.

Before leaving for the town hall, Sorina gave Grandma the little wooden box found in the attic. Grandma opened it. She took out the exercise book. She leafed through it slowly with trembling hands. She recognised her childhood handwriting, her drawings, an essay about spring with a mistake on every line. She laughed. Then she cried. Then she showed Viorica a page: a drawing of the house, with the lime tree in front, much smaller than today. She was seven. So was the lime tree.

At eleven everyone went to the commune town hall, two kilometres away, for the civil wedding. It was a small room with yellow walls, a Romanian flag, a portrait of the president and a bunch of plastic flowers. The mayor, a round man in a suit that was too tight, read out the articles of the Civil Code in Romanian, very fast. Sorina and Andrei said “da”. Julien and Ioana signed the register as godparents. Then the mayor asked whether there were any other formalities. Rose-Hélène raised her hand. She asked whether they could have eight bars of silence.

The mayor didn’t understand. Ioana explained in Romanian. The mayor thought for a moment, looking at the portrait of the president as if asking his permission. Then he shrugged and said Romanian law didn’t forbid silence. The whole room fell silent. Eight bars. Rose-Hélène counted on her fingers. On the fifth, Amina struck her little silver triangle, and Awa, in Bertrand’s arms, said “papa” very loudly in the middle of the silence. The mayor burst out laughing. He said it was the strangest wedding he had ever conducted.

Hearing Grandma’s maiden name, the mayor looked up from his register. He said his own grandfather often talked about Grandma’s father, who had been the village schoolteacher for thirty years and had taught half the commune to read. Grandma said nothing. She just nodded, very proud. Ioana learnt that day that her great-grandfather had been a schoolteacher. She thought of Odile, who had been one too, in Lyon. She thought that schoolteachers turned up everywhere in this story.

In the afternoon, the religious ceremony took place in the little wooden village church where Grandma’s parents had married in 1938. The priest, an old man with a long white beard, placed golden crowns on the couple’s heads. Julien and Ioana held the tall candles decorated with white ribbons. Then the priest led the couple three times round the altar, singing, followed by the godparents. Haruka, Farid and the Lyon group watched without understanding everything, but deeply moved. Farid said later it was like the weddings in his village in Afghanistan.

During the ceremony, when the priest asked for the rings, Henri-Ion took the little box out of his pocket so enthusiastically that it slipped out of his hands. It rolled across the church’s wooden floor under Ioana’s horrified eyes. It was Farid who caught it, with a quick movement, before it disappeared under a pew. He handed it back to Henri-Ion without a word. Henri-Ion gave it to the priest with an innocent smile. After the ceremony, Ioana told Farid he had just saved a wedding.

Back from the church, the party began under the lime tree. The village women had laid a table thirty metres long, covered with embroidered cloths and dishes: ciorbă, sarmale, cozonac, plăcinte, tomatoes from the garden, sheep’s cheese, painted eggs left over from Easter. Dan had brought țuică, the plum brandy from his village, in unlabelled bottles. Bertrand tried a small glass. He coughed for a minute. He said that was exactly what Ibrahima had felt with his cigarette.

At the start of the meal Grandma stood up to make a toast. She spoke in Romanian and Elena translated for the Lyon group. She spoke of her husband, dead for twenty-one years, who would have loved to dance under this lime tree. She spoke of her parents, married in 1938 in the same church. She said this house had waited sixty years for people to come back and celebrate in it. Then she raised her glass of țuică and said: “To the couple, to the nași, and to everyone who has come from far away to answer.” She drank her glass in one go.

A group of village musicians arrived around five: lăutari, traditional musicians, with a violin, an accordion, a double bass and a cimbalom, a kind of large stringed instrument struck with little hammers. They played fast and loud with incredible energy. Haruka had never heard anything like it. After ten minutes she took out her violin and tried to keep up. The group’s old violinist looked at her, surprised. Then he beckoned her over. They played together for an hour.

The lăutari leader was called Costel. He was sixty, with a black moustache and a violin that had belonged to his grandfather. During a break, Haruka played him Henri’s waltz. He listened once, eyes closed. Then he played it back note for note, but his own way, with ornaments, glissandos and an energy that transformed it completely. Haruka said she had never heard the waltz like that. Costel said a good melody was like a beautiful woman: every dress suited her.

Then everyone danced the hora, holding each other by the shoulders, in a big circle round the lime tree. The villagers, the Lyon group, the people from Bucharest, the children. Mr Petrescu with Elena. Gérard Thiébaut, who had arrived from Mirecourt that morning, with Isabelle. Bertrand, getting his feet wrong at every step, with Amina counting the steps aloud. Awa danced in Farid’s arms. In the middle of the circle, Grandma and Viorica, in their armchairs, beat time with their canes, laughing.

During the hora, Bertrand asked Grandma to dance. Grandma refused at first, pointing to her cane. Then she accepted, on condition he didn’t step on her feet. He stepped on her feet three times. Grandma laughed every time. Awa, who wanted to do like everyone else, tried to dance alone in the middle of the circle. She took three steps, then sat down hard on the grass, without crying. She got up. She tried again. The whole wedding party applauded her.

Around eight, when the sun began to set behind the hills, Andrei asked for silence. The lăutari stopped. Everyone sat down. Andrei said Sorina wanted to play something before night fell. The piano from the Iași school had been set up under the lime tree on a rug. Sorina sat down on the stool in her wedding dress, with a crown of lime blossom in her hair that Rose-Hélène had woven for her. She looked at Viorica. Viorica nodded. Sorina began to play Henri’s waltz.

At that same moment in Lyon, Théo had gathered the Thursday orchestra, exceptionally on a Saturday evening, in the Salle Hélène Morel. They were connected to the village by a tablet Sami held at arm’s length. They played the waltz at the same time as Sorina, with a slight delay because of the connection. Bernard Delorme had his foghorn. Inès, Sami, Léonie, Monique, Gérard the café owner and the op-ed club were there. In Dakar, Mariama and Lamine’s children were listening too, under the mango tree, on Moussa’s phone.

The whole village fell silent. The villagers didn’t know the waltz. They knew nothing of Lyon, Dakar or the landing. But they listened in silence, the way you listen to music you recognise without ever having heard it. The first verse. The second. Then the third, and Sorina lifted her hands. Eight bars. Under the lime tree of 1946, in a Moldavian village, a hundred people fell silent together. All you could hear were the birds in the branches and, far off, a dog barking.

In the Salle Hélène Morel, two thousand kilometres away, the orchestra had fallen silent at exactly the same moment as the village. On the tablet you could see the musicians motionless, bows raised. On the fifth bar in Lyon, Bernard Delorme pressed his foghorn. The sound reached the village a second late, tiny and crackling, out of the tablet. The villagers turned round, surprised. An old villager asked what it was. Ioana said it was a ship. The old man said there was no sea in Moldavia.

On the fifth bar Viorica stood up, with Ilinca’s help. She went to the piano. She held out one finger, the index finger of her right hand, and played three notes. The next three notes. Then she turned to Grandma and beckoned. Grandma stood up too, with Dan’s help. She went to the piano. Viorica took her hand. She showed her how to put two fingers, the index and middle finger, on the keys. And Grandma, who had never touched a piano in her life, played the next three notes. With two fingers. In tune.

It was the first time, as far as the whole family could remember, that Grandma had played three notes in tune. She looked at her two fingers on the keys, amazed, as if she had just discovered they belonged to her. Viorica laughed. She said she had kept her promise: she had taught her to play with two fingers. Then Haruka raised her violin and played the end of the waltz, standing under the lime tree, with Sorina at the piano. And when the last note faded, the lăutari took up the melody their own way, twice as fast, and the whole village started dancing again.

Gérard Thiébaut chose that moment to give the couple his present. It was a tiny child’s violin, a sixteenth size, the hundred and fifty-eighth he had made. He had made it from the wood of an old lime tree that had fallen the previous winter in the Vosges. He said it was for their first child, if they had one, and if it wanted to play. If not, they could hang it on the wall, like a question. Sorina blushed. Andrei said they would think about it. Grandma said in Romanian that she hoped they wouldn’t think about it too long, at her age.

Later, when night had fallen and the lanterns were lit in the lime tree, Viorica asked to speak. Ilinca brought her a chair by the piano. Everyone drew closer. Viorica took a yellowed envelope out of her bag. Everyone recognised it. It was her father’s letter, the one from 1950, the one that had slept for eighty-three years under the piano keys, the one she had always refused to read aloud. She had taken it out of the piano the day before she left, with Mr Petrescu’s help.

She said she had kept this letter to herself all her life, because she felt it was the last thing she had left of her father. But at ninety-six she had understood that the things you keep to yourself end up disappearing with you. She wanted this letter to go on living after her. So she would read it. Just once. Here, under this lime tree, on the day of her great-grandson’s wedding. She asked Andrei to translate it into French, sentence by sentence, for the Lyon group.

The letter was short. Viorica read it slowly, in Romanian, in her frail, clear voice, by the light of the lanterns. “To whoever opens this piano. Tomorrow they will take this house from us. They will take this piano. They will think they have taken everything. But music cannot be confiscated. It stays in the fingers of those who played it, and in the ears of those who heard it. If you are reading these lines, the piano has survived. So play. And if you cannot play, whistle. Someone will answer you in the end.”

Andrei translated the last sentence with difficulty. His voice was shaking. When he had finished there was a long silence under the lime tree. Nobody moved. Isabelle was crying. Julien was holding Ioana’s hand. Rose-Hélène’s eyes were wide. She said very softly that it was exactly what Grandma Odile had said. Whistle, and wait for someone to answer. Viorica smiled. She said her father and Odile had never met, but they would have had a lot to say to each other. Or rather, a lot to whistle to each other.

Mr Petrescu, who had listened to the reading sitting at the foot of the piano, said something nobody expected. He said he had held that letter in his hands in 2033, in his workshop, when he found it under the keys. He could have opened it. Nobody would ever have known. He hadn’t, out of respect. He had waited four years to find out what it said. He said it had been worth the wait. Then he added that Viorica’s father had been right: the piano had survived. He knew. He was the one who had repaired it.

Viorica folded the letter again. Then she handed it to Sorina. She said she was giving it to her. Not to put in a museum, or a drawer. To put back in the Maison Stan piano, under the keys, with Andrei’s card, when she herself was gone. For the next person to open the piano. Sorina took the letter in both hands, the way you take something very fragile. She promised. Then Grandma, who hadn’t understood a word of the French but had understood everything anyway, whistled three notes. Very loudly. Very off-key. The whole village answered.

Doina and Grandma finally settled their dispute about the sarmale. Each had made her own, on two different tables. Amina, who couldn’t help herself, organised a secret ballot, with slips of paper and a spreadsheet. Fifty-two votes for the Moldavian sarmale, fifty-two for the Bucharest ones. A perfect tie. Amina checked three times. The two women glared at each other. Then they burst out laughing and hugged. Amina noted in the spreadsheet: “A draw. As always.”

The party went on until three in the morning. The lăutari played non-stop. Haruka played with them until her fingers hurt. Henri-Ion fell asleep under the table, with the rings he had not, in the end, lost, in his pocket. Rose-Hélène taught Farid to dance the hora. Farid taught Rose-Hélène a Dari word meaning “celebration”. And at midnight Bertrand gave a wedding speech, with a printed spreadsheet Amina had prepared, listing eleven reasons why Sorina and Andrei would be happy. The twelfth row was empty. It was called “What comes next”.

Around two, Ioana went to see whether the two grandmothers wanted to go to bed. She found them on the veranda, asleep side by side in their armchairs, under the same embroidered blanket, one’s head resting on the other’s shoulder. They were still holding hands. Ioana didn’t want to wake them. She stood watching them for a while by the light of the lanterns. Then she went to fetch Julien, Isabelle and Sorina so they could see too. Nobody took a photo. Léonie Garnier, who wasn’t there, would have said it was better that way.

On Sunday, before taking the train back to Bucharest, Viorica said goodbye to Grandma on the veranda. They held hands for a long time without speaking. Then Grandma said she would expect her the following summer, under the same lime tree, for the second piano lesson, with three fingers this time. Viorica said she would come, if her health allowed. Grandma said doctors said a lot of things. Viorica laughed. She said that was exactly what she had told hers.

The Lyon group left on Monday. Before getting into the car, Rose-Hélène went alone to the lime tree. She put her hand on the bark, as she did with all lime trees. She said it was happy. Then she took an empty little bottle out of her pocket and filled it at the garden pump. She said she would pour this water at the foot of the La Duchère lime tree when she got home. That way, the two trees would know they were part of the same family.

The next morning Viorica wrote in her diary, as she had every evening since childhood, but a day late. She wrote that she hadn’t thought she would live to see that day. She wrote that if her father had lived, he would have been proud. And she wrote one last sentence, which she showed to nobody except Rose-Hélène, years later: “In the lime tree, someone is whistling three notes. I don’t know who it is. I don’t need to know. I’m going to answer.”

Viorica has kept a diary since she was a child. Here is the page written on the evening of the wedding. Notice the tenses: present, past, future perfect, past conditional. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Journal de Viorica, 1er mai 2037

This evening I am writing by the light of a lantern, under a ninety-one-year-old lime tree, in a Moldavian village I had never been to. My grandson got married today. I didn’t think I would live to see this day.

If my father had lived, he would have played a Chopin waltz. He would have been proud that Andrei was marrying a young woman who plays the piano. He would have liked, I think, for her to play his piano, the one that was taken out through the window in 1950.

Before the couple said yes, Sorina played Henri’s waltz on an old piano brought from Iași. At the silence, I played three notes with one finger. Then Ioana’s grandmother played three more, with two fingers. I had promised to teach her.
We laughed like two little girls. She is ninety-one, I am ninety-six. Between us we have a hundred and eighty-seven years of memories, and yet it seems to me that we have always known each other.
Tomorrow, when everyone has left, I will go back to Bucharest. When I have got back to my armchair, by my father’s piano, I will write what comes next. Provided I still have time.
It is late. In the lime tree, someone is whistling three notes. I don’t know who it is. I don’t need to know. I’m going to answer.
